title: Chocolate curls and shavings
subtitle: How to make chocolate curls, shavings, cigarellos, and bark splinters for cake decoration
excerpt: Chocolate curls are made by drawing a peeler or a large knife across a block of chocolate at the right temperature: cold chocolate shards, warm chocolate smears, and chocolate at about 18 to 20 degrees Celsius curls cleanly. Shavings, cigarellos, and bark splinters each require a slightly different temperature and technique.
sourceNotes: Chocolate shaving and curling techniques are standard professional patisserie skills documented in confectionery manuals and professional pastry training curricula. The temperature windows are established across the industry for couverture and cooking chocolate of 55 to 65% cocoa solids.

recipe.yieldDescription: Enough curls to decorate one 20 cm cake
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make curls up to 3 days ahead. Store on baking paper in an airtight box at around 15 degrees Celsius.

glossaryTerms.definition: Chocolate that has been melted, cooled to a specific temperature, and brought back up to create a stable crystal structure. Tempered chocolate snaps cleanly, has a gloss, and curls well when shaved.

content.text: Chocolate curls require the right block temperature and the right blade angle.

works best, but a good-quality cooking chocolate block at 18 to 20 degrees Celsius curls cleanly even without tempering. Cold chocolate from the fridge snaps into shards. Chocolate above 22 degrees smears. Temperature is the variable to watch.
Leave a 200 g block of dark chocolate at room temperature for 30 minutes in a cool kitchen, around 18 degrees Celsius.
Draw a Y-shaped vegetable peeler along the flat edge of the block with light, even pressure. The peel should lift away as a thin curl.
If it snaps, the chocolate is too cold; leave it 5 more minutes and try again. Collect finished curls on baking paper.
Large curls with a chef's knife
Hold the block of chocolate steady on a cutting board with your free hand.
Draw the blade of a large chef's knife across the block at a 45-degree angle with one long, even stroke, pressing firmly. The curl should roll away from the blade as you move.
Keep the blade warm (dry it near the hob between strokes) for longer, looser curls.
Melt 100 g of chocolate and spread it thinly across a clean marble surface or a cold baking tray to a depth of about 2 mm.
Leave until just set but still pliable, around 5 minutes.

Draw a metal scraper across the surface at a 45-degree angle with a single firm stroke; the chocolate rolls into a tube. Transfer to baking paper immediately and work quickly before the surface firms.
Spread melted chocolate thinly on baking paper and scatter toppings if using (sea salt flakes, chopped pistachios).
Leave to set fully, then snap into irregular shards by hand. The rough edges give a more natural effect than cut pieces.
Use two spoons or a soft brush to place curls rather than your fingers. Body heat melts the surface and leaves prints. Store in a cool place (not the fridge) until the cake is ready to serve.
